vertical_interpretation: Illustrative height above the mapped ellipsoid. Published MSL or AGL altitudes are used as approximate local height because this prototype has no detailed terrain model.
warning: These are not observed altitude traces. Only a few event heights are documented; all other point heights are interpolated estimates from aircraft performance and flight context.

wright-first-flight.basis: NPS reports the first hop about 8 feet above the ground; a low smooth arc connects takeoff and landing.

lindbergh-spirit-of-st-louis.basis: The Smithsonian describes a surviving barograph with climbs for weather, turbulence-induced drops, and descent near Ireland, but not digitized point heights. Control heights are illustrative.

enola-gay-hiroshima.basis: The Smithsonian documents a 31,000-foot bomb release over Hiroshima. Other heights are smooth B-29 climb, cruise, and return estimates.

earhart-solo-atlantic.basis: Lockheed Vega-era cruise-height reconstruction; no continuous altimeter record has been incorporated.

bell-x1-sound-barrier.basis: NASA reports the B-29 carrier at about 20,000 feet; NASA's X-1 account gives an approximately 43,000-foot test height. The carrier segment and rocket climb are generalized.

us-airways-1549.basis: The NTSB gives 2,818 feet AGL at the bird encounter. Other event heights are smoothed estimates along the reported radar track, not FDR samples.

concorde-ba300.basis: British Airways gives Concorde a cruise capability up to 60,000 feet; this first London-Bahrain service is illustrated with a 55,000-foot cruise estimate.

rutan-voyager.basis: Smithsonian reports an 8,000-foot economical height, 20,500 feet over Africa to avoid storms, and 3,500 feet after a late engine emergency. The intervening heights are inferred.

alcock-brown-atlantic.basis: Illustrative low-thousands-of-feet cruise for the modified Vickers Vimy; the RAF source confirms the flight, not a continuous height trace.

bleriot-channel.basis: A low-level Channel crossing is inferred from the early monoplane and the documented short route; no point altitudes are claimed.

vin-fiz-transcontinental.basis: Smithsonian records a 4,000-foot height near Imperial Junction; elsewhere short low-level legs are inferred. Named stops are treated as landings for illustration.

jannus-first-airline.basis: Illustrative low-height Benoist flying-boat crossing of Tampa Bay; the source gives duration and route but no altimeter trace.

douglas-world-cruisers.basis: Illustrative 1924 biplane cruise heights between named stations. Some anchors were overflights rather than stops, so local descents should not be read as a flight log.

southern-cross-transpacific.basis: Illustrative Fokker trimotor cruise and landing transitions on documented legs; no recorded heights were recovered.

wiley-post-solo-world.basis: The 1933 flight predated Post's 1935 pressure-suit stratospheric experiments. Heights are conservative Vega cruise estimates between stops, not the later 30,000-foot research profile.

china-clipper-airmail.basis: Illustrative Martin M-130 cruise between documented Pacific refueling stops; no altitude log is asserted.

spruce-goose.basis: The aircraft's museum reports about 25 feet over the harbor during its brief hop.

first-commercial-747.basis: A 35,000-foot long-haul 747-100 cruise is estimated from type performance; the inaugural flight's actual cleared levels are not known.

gossamer-albatross.basis: The human-powered Channel flight is shown only a few metres over water; Smithsonian confirms the route but does not provide an altitude trace.

solar-impulse-2.basis: The mission gives 8,500 metres maximum cruising altitude and a day-climb/night-descent strategy. Cycles are schematic because point timestamps are unavailable.

nc4-first-atlantic-crossing.basis: The Navy lists a 4,500-foot ceiling; lower typical flying-boat cruise is inferred between documented harbor landings.

graf-zeppelin-world-flight.basis: The Stanovoy crossing is reported near 6,000 feet; ordinary airship heights are illustrative. Only documented landing stations are treated as stops.

lucky-lady-ii-world-flight.basis: B-50 cruise and four aerial-refueling regions are documented, but refueling altitudes are not. A roughly 20,000-foot cruise with shallow refueling descents is illustrative.

sr71-coast-to-coast-record.basis: The Air Force documents SR-71 high-altitude capability; 80,000 feet is a representative record-run height, not a published altimeter trace for 6 March 1990.

air-canada-143-gimli-glider.basis: FAA reports a 41,000-foot cruise, first engine loss during descent, and second engine loss at 35,000 feet. The final powerless glide is estimated to the Gimli landing.
